Name: schema_overregularization
Title: Overregularization in LLMs: When a Stored Exception Loses to a Generalizable Rule It Contradicts
Short Hypothesis: LLMs store both broad generalizable rules/schemata (e.g., 'the plural of X is X+s', 'a country's capital is its largest city', 'company founders are CEOs') and specific exception facts that violate those rules. We hypothesize a distinct, predictable failure mode—overregularization—in which the model retrieves and produces the rule-consistent answer even when it internally stores the correct exception, because the rule pathway and the exception pathway compete and the rule wins on ambiguous or low-frequency exceptions. We predict (1) rule application and exception recall are causally dissociable pathways decodable at different depths, (2) overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions where the rule is strong, above matched baselines, and (3) suppressing the rule pathway (not amplifying the fact) selectively recovers the stored exception with high specificity, whereas ROME-style fact editing does not address the root cause.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning/generalization and memorization occupy separable-but-interacting circuits and layers (Disentangling Recall and Reasoning, 2025; Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning, 2025; Demystifying LLM Layers, 2025), that memorization builds on and coexists with generalization mechanisms with intermediate reasoning outputs computed even when a memorized label is emitted (Reason to Rote, 2025), and that a single linear direction mediates a reasoning-vs-memorization switch (LiReFs, 2025). Declarative statements causally shape generalization (Tell, don't show, 2023). All of these characterize that rule/generalization and fact/memorization mechanisms co-exist, but none identify overregularization—the rule pathway overriding a correctly-stored exception—as a concrete, predictable factual-answering failure, none causally localize the failure to rule-vs-exception competition, and none propose rule-pathway suppression as a non-destructive fix. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals (expression gating, format-bound copies, entity-candidate competition, retrieve-vs-assemble route arbitration, pre-retrieval familiarity, property collapse, premature lexicalization): here the competition is between a productive rule and a fact that violates it, mirroring the classic human overregularization phenomenon (e.g., 'goed' for 'went').
Abstract: Large language models generalize from productive rules and schemata—regular plurals, default relational patterns, statistical regularities—while also storing specific facts that violate those rules. We propose that this dual organization creates a distinct, overlooked failure mode we call overregularization: when a query targets an exception, the model produces the rule-consistent answer even though it internally stores the correct exception, because a rule-application pathway competes with and overrides an exception-recall pathway. Under this account, some knowledge failures are neither storage nor gating failures but rule-vs-exception arbitration failures, directly paralleling human overregularization ('goed' for 'went'). We build controlled rule/exception item sets across three domains—morphology (irregular inflection), factual relations with statistical defaults (e.g., capital≠largest-city, founder≠CEO), and numeric/temporal regularities—and identify exceptions that the model stores (recoverable under strong prompting or by a linear content probe) yet answers with the rule-consistent value. We test three claims. (1) Dissociability: a rule-strength probe (predicting the rule-consistent output) and an exception-content probe (predicting the correct stored exception) are separable and decodable at different layers, with rule signals emerging early. (2) Prevalence: overregularization errors concentrate on low-frequency exceptions with high rule support, above frequency- and similarity-matched baselines, and the wrong answers are disproportionately the exact rule-predicted value. (3) Intervention: suppressing the rule pathway (via a learned low-rank rule direction) recovers the stored exception with higher specificity and less collateral damage than amplifying the fact or ROME editing, and preserves correct rule application on true regulars. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating probe separability, layer-onset ordering, error-type prevalence, causal transfer, recovery rate, specificity, and fluency.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 - rule/exception items with rule-predicted and true values): Builds controlled items where a productive rule and a stored exception diverge. Data: constructed from three domains - (a) morphology: regular vs. irregular inflections (plurals, past tense) from a standard English inflection list (~2,000 irregulars available; use 1,500); (b) factual defaults with documented exceptions - capital-vs-largest-city, founder-vs-CEO, author-vs-most-famous-work - built from Wikidata (target 3,000 exception items where rule-predicted != correct); (c) numeric/temporal regularities (e.g. month-length exceptions). Per item we record the rule-predicted answer, the correct answer, and an exception flag; fewer than all candidates because each needs verified rule-vs-exception divergence. Model: Llama-3-8B (8B, decoder-only), frozen; seed 0. Systems compared: rule-predicted vs. true value per item. Decisive metric: coverage = verified exception items with single-token-first answers across the three domains (first); supporting: per-domain counts. Convincing: >=3,500 verified exception items spanning all three domains. Undecidable band: 1,500-3,500 items is thin - report reduced power. Negative: <1,500 usable exceptions means the phenomenon cannot be tested at scale here.

Experiment 2 (H1/H2 - exceptions are actually stored): Confirms the model stores each exception, so overregularization is a retrieval-not-storage failure. Data: the exception items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; storage confirmed by (i) strong retrieval prompts / few-shot demonstrations and (ii) a trainable linear content probe decoding the correct answer from the residual stream, seeds 0/1/2, conservative thresholds. Systems compared: strong-prompt recovery and content-probe recovery vs. a label-shuffle control. Decisive metric: fraction of exceptions with positive storage evidence by both criteria (first, defines the stored-exception set); supporting: content-probe AUROC. Convincing: >=50% of exceptions pass both criteria, giving a solid stored-exception set. Undecidable band: 30-50% pass means the stored set is modest and strong-prompt leakage is a risk - report conservative coverage. Negative: <30% pass, or content probe at shuffle level, means few exceptions are genuinely stored, so overregularization cannot be distinguished from ignorance.

Experiment 3 (H1 - rule and exception signals decodable at different depths): Tests that the rule signal is decodable earlier than the exception content. Data: the stored-exception set from Experiment 2. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; two trainable per-layer probes - a rule-strength probe (target: the rule-predicted token / a scalar rule-applicability score) and an exception-content probe (target: the correct answer); onset-layer test with bootstrap CIs, residualization orthogonality check, seeds 0/1/2, label-shuffle controls. Systems compared: rule vs. exception onset layers. Decisive metric: onset-layer difference (first-layer at AUROC>=0.7), rule expected earlier (first); supporting: post-residualization retained predictiveness of each. Convincing: rule onset precedes exception onset by >=3 layers with non-overlapping CIs, and each retains predictiveness after residualizing out the other (retained AUROC >=0.70). Undecidable band: a 1-3 layer gap or overlapping CIs cannot establish depth separation - defer to the causal test (Experiment 5). Negative: exception onset at/before rule, or the two collapsing under residualization, falsifies H1.

Experiment 4 (H2 - overregularization concentrates on low-frequency exceptions with strong rules): Tests the prevalence pattern. Data: errors on the stored-exception set. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; classify errors into (a) overregularization (emitted answer equals the exact rule-predicted value while the exception is stored), (b) other, (c) correct. Systems compared: overregularization rate vs. exception frequency and rule support, against a null controlling for exception-answer frequency and lexical similarity to the rule-predicted answer (logistic regression / chi-square). Decisive metric: odds ratio linking low exception frequency + high rule support to overregularization, above the matched null (first); supporting: per-domain rates. Convincing: odds ratio >=2x over the null (p<0.001) - overregularization concentrates as predicted. Undecidable band: odds ratio 1.3-2x is a modest but real concentration - report as a localized minor mode. Negative: <=1.3x or null-indistinguishable falsifies H2's concentration claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - rule suppression, not fact amplification, is the effective lever): Causally dissociates weak exception recall from an overriding rule pathway. Data: overregularization failures (target 1,500) plus true regulars (target 1,000 as a positive control). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; (a) patch the exception-content representation from a correct run into a failure, (b) suppress the rule direction (from Experiment 3) at rule-onset layers, (c) amplify the exception-content direction alone; positive control: rule suppression on true regulars must degrade their correct rule-based answers; random-direction control. Systems compared: content-patch vs. rule-suppression vs. content-amplification vs. random, plus the regulars control. Decisive metric: exception recovery under rule-suppression minus recovery under content-amplification (first, the causal signature that the rule pathway is the lever); supporting: degradation of true regulars under rule suppression (must be substantial). Convincing: rule suppression recovers >=35% of exceptions while content amplification recovers <=15% (gap >=20 points), AND rule suppression degrades true regulars by >=30% (confirming the rule pathway was manipulated). Undecidable band: a 10-20 point recovery gap, or <15% regulars degradation, means the rule pathway is only partly the lever - report weak causal support. Negative: no gap (amplification works as well), or no regulars degradation, means we did not isolate an overriding rule pathway, falsifying H1/H3's mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 - rule-suppression steering recovers exceptions selectively; editing does not address the cause): Tests a training-free rule-suppression vector against fact editing. Data: held-out overregularization failures, target 800. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen except the ROME/MEMIT comparators; a rank<=8 rule vector (mean difference of rule-dominant vs. exception-dominant matched states) subtracted, alpha swept; random-direction control; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: rule-suppression vs. exception-direction amplification vs. ROME/MEMIT editing of the exception vs. random. Decisive metric: recovered-exceptions-per-unit-collateral = recovery / accuracy drop on (i) 200 unrelated facts and (ii) held-out true regulars (first, regulars must stay correct); supporting: raw recovery, held-out perplexity. Convincing: >=40% recovery with <5% drop on unrelated facts and true regulars, beating ROME/MEMIT on recovered-per-collateral by >=1.5x. Undecidable band: a 1.0-1.5x advantage, or 5-10% regulars degradation, is parity/marginal - report with a caveat. Negative: recovery <20%, or regulars degrading >10%, falsifies the selective-recovery half of H3.

Experiment 7 (H3 generality - one rule-suppression vector transfers across families and models): Tests transfer and architecture-generality. Data: train on one domain/rule family, apply to held-out ones; reuse the Experiment 1 items per model. Model: single vector on Llama-3-8B; repeat Experiments 2-6 on GPT-J-6B and Qwen2.5-7B, frozen, identical seeds. Systems compared: cross-family transfer vs. within-family oracle; three models per decisive metric. Decisive metric: cross-family recovery rate and cross-model sign-consistency of the Experiment 4 concentration and Experiment 6 advantage (first); supporting: per-model onset gaps. Convincing: cross-family recovery >=25% and all three models show concentration and a recovery advantage >=1.2x. Undecidable band: transfer 10-25% or the pattern in 2 of 3 models is partial generality - scope accordingly. Negative: <10% transfer or majority model reversal means the mechanism is family/model-specific.

Experiment 8 (H2 - the failure is driven by rule strength versus exception weakness): Tests the source of overregularization. Data: per-item overregularization outcomes across domains. Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; regress overregularization rate on exception-answer frequency, rule productivity (fraction of the family following the rule), and the frequency ratio between rule-predicted and true answers. Systems compared: rule-strength regressors vs. an exception-frequency-only baseline. Decisive metric: partial R^2 of rule productivity + frequency ratio beyond exception frequency (first); supporting: coefficient signs. Convincing: rule-strength features add partial R^2 >=0.10 with the predicted signs (higher productivity and higher rule:exception frequency ratio raise the rate). Undecidable band: partial R^2 0.03-0.10 is a weak trend - report as suggestive. Negative: partial R^2 <0.03 means rule strength does not drive the failure, falsifying the core mechanistic claim of H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cleanly separating 'rule' from 'exception' representations may be hard when they are entangled (superposition); the causal patching and rule-suppression tests (Exp 5–6), rather than probe onset alone, are the decisive evidence, and graded results would still be informative.
Overregularization errors may be rare relative to generic errors; the frequency/similarity-matched baseline is essential and a modest but significant, well-localized effect remains publishable.
Establishing that an exception is truly 'stored' risks overestimation from strong-prompt leakage; we use conservative content-probe thresholds and held-out verification and report coverage limits.

Rule suppression could break correct rule application on genuine regulars or degrade fluency; the true-regulars specificity control (Exp 5c/6) is central and utility may be capped even if the analysis holds.
A single transferable rule-suppression vector may not exist if rules are family-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers complicate probe/logit-lens readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 6–8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
